header:
Molecular Qubit Frameworks
Molecular qubit frameworks (MQFs) are among the leading candidate materials for quantum-information chips. Molecular qubits are functional materials that use electron-spin states within molecules to store and process quantum information. Under an applied magnetic field, two controllable quantum states can be selected from the low-energy levels of a magnetic center to serve as the qubit states "0" and "1". Long-term information storage requires minimizing environmental perturbations to the electron spins and isolating the magnetic centers from one another to obtain a long coherence time. A research team successfully constructed a diluted array of molecular spin qubits by doping trace amounts of $Nd^{3+}$ magnetic spin centers into a rigid yttrium-based MOF.

2.1 The yttrium-based MOF has the formula $[C_5N_2H_{11}][Y(C_2O_4)_2]$. The cation does not coordinate to $Y^{3+}$. The MOF crystallizes in the monoclinic system with $\beta$ = 130.6°. Each $C_2O_4^{2-}$ bridges two $Y^{3+}$ ions in a $\mu_2$-$\kappa^2$O,O′;$\kappa^2$O″,O‴ mode, chelating each $Y^{3+}$ ion through two O atoms. Answer the following questions about this compound.
2.1.1 The cation of this compound contains a six-membered ring, its two nitrogen atoms have identical chemical environments, and it contains no tertiary carbon atom. Write the SMILES string for the cation.

2.3 In quantum-information storage, environmental lattice vibrations (phonon scattering) strongly perturb spin qubits and shorten their lifetimes. Theoretical studies show that, in this porous oxalate framework, the spin–lattice relaxation rate $1/T_1$ of $Nd^{3+}$ in the higher-temperature range 6.5K–8.5K is driven primarily by the combined Raman process and Orbach process and obeys the following kinetic equation:
$\frac{1}{T_1}=A_{Raman}T^7+A_{Orbach}\exp\left(-\frac{U_{eff}}{T}\right)$
Here, $A_{Raman}$ and $A_{Orbach}$ are the prefactors for the respective mechanisms, and $U_{eff}$ is the effective energy barrier of the low-lying excited state arising from strong spin–orbit coupling. The experimentally measured $U_{eff}$ for this material is 32.6 K.
The table below gives experimental spin–lattice relaxation times $T_1$ measured for the extremely dilute sample at different temperatures $T$ using a pulsed EPR spectrometer:

| 7.2 | 4.623 |
| 7.6 | 3.252 |
